text:
Last Saturday, I was dusting the bookshelf in the hallway. I pulled down a hardcover. My grandmother had given it to me years ago. The dust jacket is long gone. The spine had turned the color of weak tea. It was soft, too. I opened it, and something fell out. It was a photograph. It was small and square. It had scalloped edges. They looked like a row of tiny waves. I picked it up and turned it over. There was no date on it. No name. Just a faded chemical smell. And a thumbprint. It was faint. It was in the corner.
The image was black and white. But it must have been a bright day. A young woman was standing under a tree. She was tipping her head back, laughing. She had one hand pressing a hat to her hair. Next to her was a young man. His shirt had rolled sleeves. He was looking at her. Not the camera. It was like she was the only weather that mattered. It took me a long moment to recognize my grandmother. All I knew was her as old. Soft arms. Hard candies. Her voice crackled. It was like a radio tuned to a faraway station. But here she was. Maybe nineteen. She was radiant. Unguarded. A stranger. But I was related to her.
I sat on the floor. The book was still open on my knees. I had read this novel in college. The margins were full of my own younger certainties. How strange it was. This photograph had been living in there all along. Pressed against a story about longing and time. I had moved this book from apartment to apartment. Never looked inside. It didn't feel like an accident. More like a message. Something I wasn't ready to receive. I realized that books aren't just containers for words. They are shelves. For the selves we forget to remember.
I looked at the photograph a while. The details started to speak. The tree was an elm. Its branches were a green cathedral in the background. The hat was straw. The dress was light. Sleeveless. The young man's smile was crooked. It was sincere. I wondered who took the picture. What happened after the shutter clicked. Did they walk to a lake? Did they argue? Did they marry? Did they know how quickly the afternoon would become an artifact? My grandmother never told me about that day. Maybe she forgot. Maybe she just chose not to carry it forward. Memory is a river. We are all trying to cup it in our hands.
I didn't put the photograph back. I set it on my desk. It sits there now. Leaning against a jar of pens. Sometimes I catch it from the corner of my eye. I feel a tug. Something I cannot name. It is not exactly grief. Though it is close. It is the ache of understanding. Every old person I have loved was once a young person. One I will never meet. Every ordinary afternoon. Like this one. Is already becoming a photograph. For someone else to find. The book remains on the shelf. A little lighter now. But I like to think the photograph is finally where it belongs. Not hidden between pages. Out in the light. Reminding me that the past is never truly past. It is only waiting. Quietly. For us to open the right book and look.
